title: C++ Idioms, Gotchas & the CP Toolkit
relevance: SDE OAs and interviews commonly probe C++ STL idioms and silent gotchas that turn correct algorithms into TLE, UB, or wrong answers under contest constraints.

phases.goal: Establish core C++ utilities candidates must know: emplace, comparators, modern randomness, and small CP helpers.

must_hit.point: emplace/emplace_back construct the element in-place in the container; insert/push_back often build a temporary then move or copy it in.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts temporary construction on push_back(Node(...)) with emplace_back(args...) writing directly into container memory.

must_hit.point: std::priority_queue defaults to std::less<T> (max-heap); use std::greater<T> for a min-heap.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the default comparator and how greater flips heap order.

must_hit.point: Since C++14, std::less<> (and similar) can be transparent, enabling heterogeneous lookup such as finding a const char* in a set of std::string without building a temporary string.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions omitting the template argument and gives a string-literal find example.

must_hit.point: Prefer <random> engines like std::mt19937 (32-bit) or std::mt19937_64 (64-bit) over legacy rand(), which is predictably flawed and low-quality.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects rand(), names mt19937 / mt19937_64 and ties randomness to avoiding worst-case behavior or adversarial hashes.

must_hit.point: assert catches false conditions by terminating; __int128 helps avoid overflow on intermediate 64-bit multiplies but needs custom I/O; std::tie unpacks pairs/tuples and supports lexicographical multi-field compares (pre-C++17 structured bindings).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names all three utilities and the __int128 I/O caveat plus tie for lex compare.

probes: When would you use emplace_back instead of push_back, and how do you turn a priority_queue into a min-heap?
Why prefer mt19937 over rand() in competitive programming?

hints.1: Think about where the object is constructed and what comparator priority_queue uses by default.
hints.2: In-place construction vs temporary; less vs greater; <random> vs rand().
hints.3: emplace_back builds in container memory; greater<T> yields a min-heap; mt19937/mt19937_64 replace low-quality rand().

phases.goal: Explain the concrete failure modes behind the classic STL and I/O bugs that cause wrong answers, UB, or TLE.

must_hit.point: map/unordered_map operator[] on a missing key silently default-inserts; use count, find, or at for read-only checks.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes silent insertion and names count/find/at as safe alternatives.

must_hit.point: multiset.erase(val) erases every equal element; erase a single occurrence via an iterator from find.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States all-vs-one erase behavior and the find-then-erase-iterator fix.

must_hit.point: A sort comparator must be a strict weak ordering: equal elements must compare false; using <= instead of < yields undefined behavior.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links <= in a comparator to UB (segfault or infinite loop) and requires < for equals.

must_hit.point: mid=(l+r)/2 can overflow; prefer l+(r-l)/2. Plain 1<<k overflows when k is at least 31 because 1 is a 32-bit int; use 1LL<<k for a 64-bit shift base.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives both overflow patterns and the corrected midpoint and 1LL forms.

must_hit.point: Default unordered_map hashing is deterministic and can be collision-attacked into per-op O(n) and TLE; mitigate with a randomized custom hash or fall back to map at O(log n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains adversarial collisions and names custom seeded hash or std::map as fixes.

must_hit.point: std::endl writes a newline and flushes; heavy flushing (e.g. on the order of 10^5 lines) can TLE—prefer '\n'. vector<bool> stores bit proxies, so bool&/pointers to elements fail; use vector<char> or vector<int> when real references are needed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates endl flush cost from vector<bool> proxy semantics and the char/int alternative.

must_hit.point: vector growth can reallocate and dangle prior element references; erase invalidates iterators (and later ones in a vector)—update with it=c.erase(it). cin>> leaves a trailing newline that a following getline may consume as an empty string; consume whitespace (e.g. cin>>ws) first.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Covers reallocation dangling refs, erase return-value loop pattern, and cin/getline leftover newline.

probes: What goes wrong if you check map membership with m[key], and how do you erase only one copy from a multiset?
Why can (l+r)/2 and 1<<k both fail, and why is endl dangerous on large output?

hints.1: Separate silent mutation, erase-by-value, overflow, and flush costs.
hints.2: operator[] inserts; erase(val) clears all equals; midpoint sum and 32-bit shift bases overflow; endl flushes.
hints.3: Use count/find/at; erase(find(val)); l+(r-l)/2 and 1LL<<k; print with '\n'.

phases.goal: Weigh idioms where the file states when one choice wins over another.

must_hit.point: Prefer emplace/emplace_back for complex objects (custom structs, strings) to skip extra copies/moves; for primitive ints the gain is negligible.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States complex-object benefit and that int performance difference is negligible.

must_hit.point: Against adversarial unordered_map TLE, choose a randomized custom hash for average O(1) behavior, or accept map's O(log n) as a simpler safe fallback.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Frames custom hash vs map as the security/simplicity tradeoff from the file.

must_hit.point: Contest macros (e.g. all(x)) save keystrokes but hurt readability and debugging if overused; fast I/O is mandatory when input/output exceeds 10^5 operations.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Balances macro brevity against readability and ties sync_with_stdio/tie to the 10^5 I/O threshold.

probes: When is emplace worth it versus push_back, and when would you abandon unordered_map for map?
How do you decide between macros for speed of typing and keeping code debuggable?

hints.1: Think object cost, hash attacks, and contest vs maintainability.
hints.2: Complex types favor emplace; collisions favor custom hash or map; macros help only if used sparingly; large I/O needs fast setup.
hints.3: emplace for structs/strings; custom hash or map under attack; light macros; fast I/O above 10^5 ops.

phases.goal: Apply the CP toolkit: templates, graph/matrix reading, and the 10^8 operations complexity heuristic.

must_hit.point: A typical CP template disables sync_with_stdio and unties cin, uses typedefs/macros sparingly, and loops solve() across test cases.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false), cin.tie(NULL), and a multi-test solve loop.

must_hit.point: Pre-size matrices and adjacency lists before filling; for undirected graphs push both directions, and adj(nodes+1) supports 1-indexing.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Prefers pre-allocation over repeated push_back growth and describes bidirectional edges plus 1-based adj sizing.

must_hit.point: Mental model: about 10^8 basic ops per second—e.g. N≤10 allows N! or 2^N; N≤20 allows 2^N; N≤10^4 allows N^2; N≤10^5 needs N log N or N; N≤10^9 needs log N or constant time.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recites the 10^8 rule and matches the listed N thresholds to the stated complexities without inventing extras.

probes: Walk through a minimal contest main: what I/O setup and structure do you use?
Given N up to 10^5, what time complexities are safe under the 10^8 operations rule?

hints.1: Template I/O flags and constraint-to-complexity mapping.
hints.2: sync_with_stdio/tie plus solve loop; preallocate graphs; map N bands to allowed big-O.
hints.3: Fast I/O + while(t--) solve(); pre-sized grid/adj; at 10^5 need O(N log N) or O(N) under ~10^8 ops/s.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Use emplace when constructing complex objects in-place to avoid temporaries and extra copies/moves; for primitive ints the difference is negligible.
Default unordered_map can TLE under adversarial collisions; a randomized custom hash restores practical average-case speed, while map is a simpler O(log n) fallback.
endl flushes after the newline and can TLE on massive output; use '\n' and let the buffer flush naturally.
vector<bool> saves space via bit packing but returns proxies you cannot take a real bool& or pointer to; use vector<char> or vector<int> when references matter.
Macros like all(x) cut typing in timed contests but excessive macros destroy readability and make debugging harder; use them judiciously.

gotchas.trap: Using m[key] to test membership in map/unordered_map.
gotchas.correction: operator[] default-inserts; use count, find, or at for read-only checks.

gotchas.trap: Calling multiset.erase(val) intending to remove one occurrence.
gotchas.correction: erase(val) removes all equals; erase(ms.find(val)) removes one.

gotchas.trap: Sorting with a comparator that uses <=.
gotchas.correction: Violates strict weak ordering and causes UB; equal elements must return false—use <.

gotchas.trap: Computing mid as (l+r)/2 or shifting with 1<<k for large k.
gotchas.correction: Use l+(r-l)/2; use 1LL<<k because plain 1 is a 32-bit int and overflows when k is at least 31.

gotchas.trap: Relying on default unordered_map under adversarial tests.
gotchas.correction: Deterministic hashing can degrade to O(n) per op; use a randomized custom hash or switch to map.
endl flushes every time; use '\n' to avoid TLE.

gotchas.trap: Taking a bool& or pointer into vector<bool>.
gotchas.correction: Elements are proxies, not real bools; pass by value or store char/int.

gotchas.trap: Holding a reference into a vector across push_back.
gotchas.correction: Reallocation invalidates references; re-index via v[i] instead of caching refs.

gotchas.trap: Erasing inside a loop without updating the iterator.
gotchas.correction: erase invalidates iterators; assign it = c.erase(it) (and only ++it when not erasing).
Trailing newline left by >> makes getline read an empty string; consume whitespace first (e.g. cin>>ws).
